newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Renault hit by EU, workers' anger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Renault hit by EU, workers' anger.

text.p: The political cost of French car maker Renault SA's decision to close its Belgian plant mounted on Thursday when the European Commission blocked subsidies to its Spanish operation and angry workers demonstrated at its Paris headquarters.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert, a Belgian Socialist, said he had blocked Spanish government subsidies for a Renault plant in Vallodolid, Spain, until the company changed its attitude on closing the Vilvoorde plant near Brussels.

"It is of course absurd that they close a profitable company such as Vilvoorde and carry out additional investment in Spain with government aid," he said. EU officials said 500 million Belgian francs ($14.1 million) was at stake.
In Paris, trade union delegates stormed out of Renault's works council after management refused to allow a representative of the Belgian workforce to address the meeting.
Some 300 workers from Vilvoorde came to Paris to protest to Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer, who offered to meet their leader but would not let him address the French works council.
Alongside 600 French workers they marched through the Paris suburb of Boulogne-Billancourt, home of Renault's headquarters, chanting "same boss, same battle" and "Renault solidarity".

The announcement of the closure in June of the recently modernised plant in Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene's home town, with the loss of 3,100 direct jobs, has triggered widespread anger in Belgium and France.
Renault has also announced plans to cut more than 2,700 jobs in France this year, but a spokeswoman said the company could transfer some of the Belgian workers to factories in France.
The idea was discussed at a meeting between protesting Belgian workers and the manager of Renault's Douai plant in northern France on Wednesday, she said.

Trade unions at Renault in France, Belgium and Spain -- but not Portugal -- plan a one-hour work stoppage on Friday in protest against "downsizing" by the smallest of Europe's six car manufacturers, faced with shrinking domestic demand, production overcapacity and a stiff price war.
Renault is expected to announce a 1996 operating loss of up to three billion French francs on March 20.
Belgian works council leader Raymond Smulders read a defiant statement to a rally near the company's headquarters.
"Mr Schweitzer, the decision to close Vilvoorde is a cowardly, unproductive and uneconomical decision. I can assure you that we will fight till the end if we must," he declared.

"We are ready to discuss all possibilities of keeping the production site in Vilvoorde. Until then, we are going to keep our 'war chest', which is worth quite a lot," he said, referring to the stock of new cars which workers occupying the factory have said they have taken control of.

French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, alarmed by the Belgian backlash, summoned Schweitzer on Wednesday and, without calling into question the industrial logic of closing the plant, urged Renault to open immediate talks with the Belgian workforce and authorities on cushioning the human cost.

Schweitzer said in a statement on Thursday: "I want to meet a Belgian delegation as soon as possible. I regret the conditions did not make that possible this morning. I continue to make every effort so contact can be established."
South Korean car maker KIA meanwhile denied a Belgian press report that it was considering buying the Vilvoorde plant.

Financial daily De Financieel-Economische Tijd quoted Jong Chung, KIA Motors Europe's managing director, as saying at the Geneva car show that his firm first had to review the books at Renault Industrie Belgique before making a final decision.
But a spokesman in Seoul said the company had never discussed the idea either internally or with Renault.
"All Korean companies are interested. But there has been no discussion of a takeover within the company or with Renault," he said. ($ = 35.34 Belgian Francs)
